what choosing your own hours amounts to
what motivators are properties of

sections.title: Job Enrichment
sections.keyIdea: Job enrichment makes the work harder and adds responsibility. It is the one method on the list that is a Herzberg motivator by construction.

body.text: **Job enrichment** is adding harder tasks and more responsibility to a job — harder tasks and more responsibility, not more tasks. The distinction is the whole of the next subsection, and it is where marks are most often lost.

It is the method Herzberg's theory predicts directly. His motivators are achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility and advancement, and enrichment adds two of them — the work itself and responsibility — by changing what the job consists of.

At Sabari Textiles that means a machinist who also inspects their own output and signs it off has a richer job: the work is harder, the responsibility is real, and the firm has moved inspection to the person who can fix the fault.

Its cost is training and its risk is the worker who does not want it. A job made harder without the training to do it is a job somebody fails at, and enrichment offered to somebody worried about their contract is aimed at Maslow's fourth level while the second is unmet.

realExample.text: A machinist who signs off their own quality has a harder job, and the firm has one fewer inspection queue, because the person who made the fault is now the person who finds it.

sections.misconception: Students use enrichment and enlargement interchangeably. Enrichment changes the DIFFICULTY and the responsibility; enlargement adds tasks at the same difficulty. Only the first reaches a Herzberg motivator, and calling enlargement enrichment is the commonest error in this sub-topic.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed chains of reasoning showing a range of causes and effects, leading to a supported judgement, for 20 marks. An Evaluate of a motivation package is expected to weigh the financial methods against the non-financial ones and conclude for a particular firm.

recall.prompt: Sort each change to a machinist's job by whether it raises the DIFFICULTY, which is what enrichment means:

groups.name: Harder, and more responsible
items: Being the one who decides whether a batch may ship
Choosing the sequence the week's orders are run in
groups.why: Difficulty and responsibility have both risen, which is enrichment — and responsibility is one of Herzberg’s five motivators.

groups.name: Bigger, and no harder
items: Adding the labelling to a job that was only sewing
Taking on the box-stacking as well
groups.why: More of the same difficulty is not enrichment at all, whatever it is called: nothing has been added that could reach the second scale.

sections.title: Job Rotation and Job Enlargement
sections.keyIdea: Rotation moves a worker between jobs of the same difficulty; enlargement adds tasks of the same difficulty to one job. Neither adds responsibility.

body.text: The last two of the eight non-financial methods are the two that look like enrichment and are not, because neither changes the DIFFICULTY of the work.

**Job rotation** is moving staff between jobs at the same level of difficulty A machinist who spends alternate weeks at the cutting bench is rotating. It relieves boredom, and it produces multi-skilling as a side effect — chapter 1's first form of flexibility, arriving through a motivation method.
**Job enlargement** is adding more tasks at the same level of difficulty to one job A machinist who also labels and boxes what they have sewn has an enlarged job. The work is broader and no harder.

On Herzberg's scales, neither reaches the second one: nothing about either adds achievement, recognition or responsibility. Both can be received as more work for the same pay, and enlargement especially — which is why the honest summary is that rotation treats boredom and enlargement treats a staffing gap, and enrichment is the only one of the three that treats motivation.

realExample.text: A packer moved between three benches in a month is less bored and no more responsible, and the firm has quietly acquired somebody who can cover all three when anyone is away.

sections.misconception: Students write that all three "job" methods motivate. Only enrichment adds responsibility, and a worker given more tasks at the same difficulty and the same pay usually experiences it as exactly that — which is why enlargement has a reputation for backfiring.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by relevant knowledge. Naming which of the three a case describes is the knowledge; saying what it therefore does to motivation is the explanation, and the marks are on the second part.

recall.prompt: Match each change to a packer's job to the method it is, and to what it does about motivation:

pairs.left: Also inspects and signs off the boxes they pack
pairs.right: Enrichment — responsibility added, so a motivator
pairs.why: Signing off means being answerable for the result, which is responsibility, and responsibility is on Herzberg’s second scale.

pairs.left: Also labels the boxes as well as packing them
pairs.right: Enlargement — more tasks, no more responsibility
pairs.why: Labelling is no harder than packing, so the job is broader and nothing has been added that could motivate.

pairs.left: Packs for a fortnight, then works the cutting bench
pairs.right: Rotation — different tasks, same difficulty
pairs.why: Moving between jobs relieves boredom without changing what the worker is answerable for.

pairs.left: Is trained on the cutting bench for when cover is needed
pairs.right: Multi-skilling — a capability the firm draws on
pairs.why: Multi-skilling is the capability rather than the movement: the firm holds it in reserve and uses it when it needs cover.

takeaway: Piecework and commission are set to equal the $360 basic week exactly: the difference is risk.
Piecework and commission move the risk onto the worker; bonus and profit share reward a group.
Delegation passes the AUTHORITY, not only the task. Without it nothing is delegated.
Enrichment raises difficulty and responsibility; rotation and enlargement do not.
Only enrichment, delegation, consultation and empowerment reach Herzberg's second scale.

content.title: Leadership

sections.title: Management and Leadership
sections.keyIdea: Management is concerned with the work getting done and takes its authority from the post. Leadership is concerned with where the firm is going.

body.text: 1.3.4 · 5a has one bullet — "the distinction between management and leadership" — and it is the chapter's opening idea rather than an aside, because the four styles that follow are styles of taking DECISIONS and the last leaf is about a founder who cannot make the change.

**Management** is about the work getting done: allocating it, checking it, and solving what goes wrong this week. Its authority comes from the POST — a supervisor is obeyed because they are the supervisor.

**Leadership** is about where the firm is going and why: setting a direction and persuading people to follow it. Its authority comes from the PERSON, which is why it can exist without a post and why a post does not confer it.

The same person usually does both, which is what makes the distinction hard to see and worth drawing. A supervisor allocating 5 machinists to 5 machines is managing; the same supervisor persuading them to accept a new shift pattern is leading, and only one of those two jobs is in the job description.

realExample.text: The person a workforce actually listens to during a change is often not the person whose title says they should be, which is the distinction in one observation.

sections.misconception: Students write that managers are junior and leaders are senior. It is not a rank: a Managing Director doing next week's rota is managing, and a machinist who talks the floor round to a new method is leading. The difference is the horizon and where the authority comes from.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define as requiring the meaning of a term or phrase. Two marks for the distinction means naming what each is concerned with — the work, and the direction — rather than describing one and implying the other.

recall.prompt: Sort each thing somebody at Sabari does by whether it is management or leadership:

groups.name: Management
items: Putting 5 machinists on 5 machines for the week
Signing off the quality records before an order ships
Redrawing next month's rota around a public holiday
groups.why: All three are about the work getting done this week, and the authority to do them comes with the post.

groups.name: Leadership
items: Convincing the machinists that an unfamiliar method is worth trying
Deciding the firm's future is in school uniforms rather than shirts
groups.why: Both are about where the firm is going and about persuading people to go there, which is authority that comes from the person.

sections.title: Autocratic Leadership
sections.keyIdea: The autocratic leader decides alone and tells. It is fast and it is right where speed matters or where staff do not yet know the work.

body.text: 1.3.4 · 5b names four styles and they differ in exactly one thing: **who takes the decision**. They run in the specification's order from the leader alone to the staff alone, and the four subsections that follow take them in that order.
**Autocratic**: the leader decides and tells. No consultation, and the reasons need not be given.

What it is for: speed, and situations where the staff genuinely do not know enough to contribute. A fire, a safety failure, a new starter's first week, an order that has to ship tonight — in all four, asking 5 machinists what they think costs more than it adds.

What it costs is everything the last chapter was about. Nobody is delegated to, nobody is consulted, nobody is empowered, so no motivator on Herzberg's second scale is available at all — and a firm led this way permanently has trained its staff not to decide, which is expensive the first time a decision has to be taken without the leader.

realExample.text: A supervisor who stops the line and reassigns everybody the moment a machine catches fire is being autocratic and is right; the same supervisor choosing next month's shift pattern the same way is not.

sections.misconception: Students write that autocratic leadership is bad management. The specification asks for it as a style, and there are cases where it is the correct one — speed, danger, and staff who do not yet know the work. Say which case before judging.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a chain of reasoning that considers the relative importance of factors, leading to a supported judgement, for 10 marks in Units 1 and 2. Assessing a style means weighing the situation against the staff, not listing advantages.

recall.prompt: Sort each situation by whether an autocratic decision is the right call or the wrong one:

groups.name: Autocratic is right
items: Smoke is coming from a machine and everyone has to move now
A customer needs the order tonight and the running order must change
Somebody has never used this machine before and is standing at it
groups.why: Speed matters more than agreement, or the staff do not yet know enough to contribute — which is exactly what the style is for.

groups.name: Autocratic is wrong
items: Settling the shift pattern for next month with 25 people affected
Working out the best way to lay out a bench nobody has used yet
groups.why: There is time, and the people who work the line know more about it than the leader does, so deciding alone produces a worse decision as well as an unpopular one.

sections.title: Paternalistic Leadership
sections.keyIdea: The paternalistic leader still decides, but explains the decision and weighs what it does to the staff. It buys loyalty and does not transfer authority.

body.text: The second style in 1.3.4 · 5b is the one most often left out of a list of four, and the one most often mistaken for a softer version of the first.

**Paternalistic**: the leader decides, as an autocrat does, and then **explains the decision and takes the staff's interests into account in making it**. The authority does not move. What changes is that the reasons are given and the effect on the staff is part of the calculation.

That makes it a separate style rather than a softer word for autocratic, and the test is a question: who decided? If the answer is the leader, it is not democratic, however consultative it felt. If the reasons were given and the staff's position was weighed, it is not autocratic either.

What it buys is loyalty and trust, and it works where the staff believe the leader is acting in their interest — a long-standing workforce, a firm that has looked after people before. What it costs is that nobody learns to decide: the staff are looked after rather than trusted, so the motivators of delegation and empowerment stay unavailable.

realExample.text: A firm that moves a shift pattern, explains exactly why, and adjusts it for the people with the longest journeys has decided paternalistically: the decision was never the staff's, and their position changed it.

sections.misconception: Students treat paternalistic as democratic because the leader explained themselves. Explaining a decision is not sharing it. The test is who decided — and under a paternalistic style the answer is still the leader.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by relevant knowledge. The knowledge here is the definition and the cause is the loyalty; an answer that describes a kindly manager without the retained authority has not defined the style.

recall.prompt: Sort each thing a leader does by whether it is autocratic or paternalistic, which are the only two styles so far:

groups.name: Autocratic
items: Tells the floor the rota has changed and does not say why
Refuses to discuss the new running order with anyone
groups.why: The decision is the leader’s and nothing is explained or weighed, which is the defining case of the autocratic style.

groups.name: Paternalistic
items: Sets the rota, gives the reason, and keeps one person off the early shift after hearing why they asked
Decides the order alone, having first worked out which bench it would hurt
groups.why: The decision is still the leader’s — the difference is that the reasons were given and the staff’s position changed the outcome.

sections.title: Democratic Leadership
sections.keyIdea: The democratic leader decides with the staff, or lets them decide. It is slower, and it is right where the staff know the work better than the leader.

body.text: **Democratic**: the leader decides WITH the staff, or hands the decision to them. This is the first style on the list where the authority actually moves, which is why it is the first that can motivate.

What it is for: decisions where the staff know more than the leader. Nobody knows how a sewing line should be arranged better than the 5 people who work it, and a decision taken with them is a better decision as well as a more popular one.

It also delivers the motivators of the last chapter by construction. Being consulted is Mayo's finding; being trusted to decide is delegation; the responsibility that comes with it is on Herzberg's second scale. None of that costs a wage.

What it costs is time, and it fails in two specific cases: where the decision is urgent, and where the staff do not know enough to take it. Consulting new starters about a method none of them has used yet produces a decision nobody should act on and a leader who looks unsure.

realExample.text: A cutting room asked how to sequence a difficult order produces a sequence the supervisor would not have thought of, and then holds to it, because it was theirs.

sections.misconception: Students write that democratic leadership is the best style. It needs staff who know the work and time to reach a decision, and it is the wrong style for an emergency or a new team. The specification asks for four styles because four situations need them.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss as requiring logical chains of reasoning in context showing causes and effects, with a brief conclusion, for 8 marks. Context decides which style is right, so a Discuss that never mentions the firm in the extract cannot reach a conclusion.

recall.prompt: A supervisor asks 5 machinists how to sequence a difficult order and adopts their answer. Work out what the style has delivered:
template: The decision has moved to the staff, so the style is ___
Being trusted to decide is the non-financial method called ___
And it costs the firm nothing in wages, which puts it on Herzberg's ___ scale
hints: which of the four styles moves the decision
the method that passes authority with a task
hygiene is the first one

sections.title: Laissez-Faire Leadership
sections.keyIdea: The laissez-faire leader sets the goal and leaves the staff to it. With expert, self-directed staff it works; without them it is abdication.

body.text: **Laissez-faire**: the leader sets the objective and leaves the staff to decide everything else. It is the far end of the list — the staff decide, and the leader is not in the room.

The condition it needs is expertise. A design team, a research group, a workshop of time-served specialists: people who know the work better than any leader could and who expect to be left to it. For them, anything else is interference and a reason to leave.

The line between this style and abdication is whether **a goal was set**. A leader who says the line must run 60 hours this week and leaves the pattern to the team is laissez-faire; a leader who says nothing is absent, and the two look identical from a distance until something goes wrong.

Applied to the wrong staff it is the most expensive style on the list. Leaving 5 new machinists to work out a method produces four methods, none of them checked, and the quality problem arrives at the customer rather than at the supervisor.

realExample.text: A group of experienced specialists given an objective and a deadline organises itself better than any instruction would have; the same freedom given to a new team produces four ways of doing one job.

sections.misconception: Students treat laissez-faire as a leader doing nothing. The style includes setting the goal, and the goal is what separates it from absence. A question asking whether a leader was laissez-faire or absent is asking whether anybody said what the objective was.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Analyse focuses on depth rather than breadth and does not include evaluation. A chain on laissez-faire runs from the staff's expertise to the quality of the decisions they take, and stops before judging the style.

recall.prompt: Match each leader to the style it is, by asking whether a goal was set and who chose the method:

pairs.left: Says the line must run 60 hours and leaves the pattern to the team
pairs.right: Laissez-faire — goal set, method theirs
pairs.why: A goal exists and the method is the team’s, which is the whole definition of the style.

pairs.left: Says nothing at all and is not seen for a fortnight
pairs.right: Absent — no goal was ever set
pairs.why: With no objective there is nothing for the staff to organise around, and the two look identical until something goes wrong.

pairs.left: Sets the hours and the pattern and announces both
pairs.right: Autocratic — both decisions kept
pairs.why: Neither the objective nor the method left the leader, which is the autocratic case.

pairs.left: Sets the hours, explains why, and adjusts for long journeys
pairs.right: Paternalistic — decision kept, staff weighed
pairs.why: The decision never moved, and the reasons and the staff’s position both entered it — explaining is not sharing.

sections.title: From Entrepreneur to Leader
sections.keyIdea: A founder decides everything and knows everyone. A leader of 31 people cannot, so the move requires delegating, structuring and leading through others.

body.text: The last leaf of the topic, 1.3.4 · 5c, asks why **moving from entrepreneur to leader is difficult**. Everything in the previous five chapters is the answer.

A founder with four staff does every job: recruits, trains, decides, sells and leads, and their authority comes from being the person who started it. Nothing has to be structured, because the founder is the structure.

At 31 people none of that survives. Somebody has to be recruited rather than known, so recruitment costs $10,800 a post. Decisions have to be delegated, because one person cannot take 31 people's decisions. A hierarchy has to exist, so authority starts coming from the POST rather than from the person — and that is the transition, in one sentence.

Which is why it is hard for the specific reason the specification implies: the skills that built the firm are the ones now in the way. Deciding fast was an advantage at four people and is a bottleneck at 31; knowing everything personally was the founder's edge and is now the thing preventing anybody else from being trusted. **The founder has to stop doing what made them successful**, on the evidence of nothing going wrong yet.

realExample.text: A firm whose founder still authorises every discount at thirty staff has not failed at anything: it has outgrown the one habit that worked best when there were four of them.

sections.misconception: Students write that the founder "needs to learn to delegate", which is the conclusion and not the difficulty. The difficulty is that delegating means accepting worse decisions in the short run from people still learning to take them, and doing it before anything has visibly gone wrong.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed, coherent chains of reasoning showing a range of causes and effects, leading to a supported judgement, for 20 marks. This leaf reaches across the whole topic, which is why it is the section's 20-mark question.

recall.prompt: Put the stages of Sabari's growth in order, from the founder doing every job to a firm of 31 led through others:
correctOrder: Four staff, and one person is doing all five jobs at once
Strangers start being hired, and hiring them costs money
There are more decisions in a week than one person can take
A supervisor is obeyed because of the post, not the person
why: At four staff nothing has to be structured, because the founder is the structure — and this is the position everything else is a departure from.
The first thing growth breaks is personal knowledge: a firm hiring strangers has to pay to find and assess them.
Once there are more decisions than one person can take, they have to move — and they move to people who are still learning to take them.
The transition is complete when the firm works because of the posts rather than because of the founder, which is the last thing to change and the hardest.

takeaway: Management is the work and comes from the post; leadership is the direction, from the person.
The four styles differ in ONE thing: who takes the decision.
Paternalistic still decides — it explains, and weighs the staff. Explaining is not sharing.
Laissez-faire sets the goal. A leader who sets no goal is absent, not laissez-faire.
From entrepreneur to leader: authority stops coming from the person and starts coming from the post.

notes.title: Approaches to Staffing
notes.keyIdea: Asset or cost, the five forms of flexible workforce, dismissal against redundancy, and the two ways pay is agreed.

items.text: Staff as an asset — spending on people and expecting the spending back as productivity, quality and retention.
Staff as a cost — buying labour as cheaply as the work allows and replacing people when they leave.
Flexible workforce — multi-skilling, part-time and temporary, zero-hour contracts, flexible hours and home working, outsourcing.
Dismissal — the contract ends because of the PERSON: conduct or capability. The post remains.
Redundancy — the contract ends because the POST has gone. Statutory redundancy pay is due.
Collective bargaining — a union negotiating one agreement covering all its members.
Asset or cost turns on how long the job takes to learn: a leaver takes months of learning with them and takes a morning's with them.
Part-time, temporary and zero-hour shift the same risk — that demand is low — in increasing amounts from the firm to the worker.
Outsourcing turns a fixed wage bill into a variable one: 25 machinists at $36,000 is $900,000 a year whether orders come or not.
The test for dismissal or redundancy is what the firm does next week: if the post is advertised, it was a dismissal.
Individual or collective follows from how alike the jobs are. 25 identical machinists are described accurately by one agreement; a rare designer is not.

takeaway: Asset or cost is a strategy and the right answer depends on the job.
Five forms of flexibility; only multi-skilling keeps the same hours and people.
Dismissal is the PERSON, redundancy is the POST.

notes.title: Recruitment, Selection and Training
notes.keyIdea: Internal against external recruitment, the $10,800 cost of filling one post, and the three types of training.

items.text: Internal recruitment — filling a post from among the people already employed.
External recruitment — filling it from the labour market, usually through advertising or an agency.
Induction training — given on arrival: the job, the place, the people and the rules
On-the-job training — learning while doing the work, alongside somebody who already does it
Off-the-job training — learning away from the work, on a course or at a provider

One supervisor on $36,000: advertising the post $1,200, agency fee $5,400, managers' time $900, induction training $900, off-the-job course $600, output lost learning $1,800 — total $10,800, which is 30% of the salary.
By stage: recruitment $6,600, selection $900, training $3,300.
Internal recruitment saves the $5,400 agency fee and MOVES the vacancy one level down rather than removing it.
Induction is for three things: less time before the person is productive, fewer early mistakes, fewer early leavers.
On-the-job costs $1,800 of lost output and produces no invoice; off-the-job costs a $600 fee and does. The larger cost is the invisible one.

takeaway: One post costs $10,800 to fill — 30% of the salary it pays.
Internal recruitment moves a vacancy down a level; it does not remove one.
The biggest training cost is output nobody invoices for.

notes.title: Organisational Design
notes.keyIdea: Hierarchy, chain of command, span of control, centralisation, and the three types of structure — with 31 people drawn two ways.

items.text: Hierarchy — the levels of authority in a firm, from the top to the shop floor
Chain of command — the route an instruction travels down those levels, counted in links
Span of control — how many people report directly to one manager
Centralised and decentralised — whether decisions are taken at the top or passed down the hierarchy
Tall, Flat, Matrix — the three types of structure. A matrix lays a project across the functions, so somebody has two managers.
A span of s over L levels reaches (s^L − 1) ÷ (s − 1) people. (2^5 − 1) ÷ 1 = 31 and (5^3 − 1) ÷ 4 = 31.
The chain of command is LINKS, one fewer than levels: 5 levels give 4 links, 3 give 2.
Tall: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31, 15 managers and 16 machinists, wage bill $1,656,000.
Flat: 1 + 5 + 25 = 31, 6 managers and 25 machinists, wage bill $1,332,000.
So flattening moves 9 posts from supervising to making and saves $324,000 = 9 × $36,000, at unchanged headcount.
Tall or flat is one choice and centralised or decentralised is another: the chart shows the levels and says nothing about who decides.

takeaway: The chain of command is counted in LINKS, one fewer than levels.
31 people, span 2 or span 5: same firm, 9 posts moved.
Delayering removes levels, not people. It widens every remaining span.

notes.title: Motivation in Theory
notes.keyIdea: Why motivation matters to a business, and the four theorists the specification names.

items.text: Taylor — scientific management.
Mayo — human relations theory.
Maslow — hierarchy of needs.
Herzberg — two-factor theory.
Hygiene factor — something that can stop dissatisfaction and cannot cause satisfaction. Pay is one.
Motivator — something that can cause satisfaction: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement.
Motivation reaches the accounts four ways: productivity, retention, quality, absenteeism. Holding losses to 1 instead of 4 saves $32,400.
Taylor: money motivates, so study the job, standardise the method, train everybody in it and pay by the piece.
Mayo: output rose when conditions changed AND when they were changed back, so what mattered was the attention and the group.
Maslow: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation. A level only motivates once the one below it is met.
Herzberg: TWO scales. Hygiene runs to "not dissatisfied"; only motivators reach satisfied, and all of them are properties of the work.
Which is why $18 a week changes little and job enrichment costs nothing and changes a lot.

takeaway: Name the route: productivity, retention, quality or absenteeism.
"Mayo proved money doesn't motivate" is false. He found the group matters too.
Herzberg is TWO scales. Hygiene cannot reach satisfied.

notes.title: Motivation in Practice
notes.keyIdea: Five financial methods and eight non-financial ones, with one worker's pay worked out under each of the five.

items.text: Piecework, Commission, Bonus, Profit share, Performance-related pay — the five financial methods the specification names.
Delegation — passing a task AND the authority to decide how it is done.
Empowerment — a standing authority over how the work is done, within limits.
Job enrichment — harder tasks and more responsibility. The only one of the three "job" methods that motivates.
Job rotation / enlargement — different tasks / more tasks, both at the SAME difficulty.

A standard week is 40 hours at $9 = $360. Piecework (240 units at $1.50) and commission (4% of $9,000) REPLACE that wage and are set to equal it; the bonus, the profit share and performance pay ADD to it.
Piecework at 200 units pays $300 and at 280 pays $420; commission at $7,500 pays $300. Both move the risk to the worker.
Bonus: 10% of the $4,680 quarter is $468, or $36 a week — all-or-nothing on a target.
Profit share: 5% of $111,600 is $5,580, split 31 ways = $180 each, and settled once a year.
Performance pay: 5% on $9 gives $9.45 an hour, $378 a week — permanent, and available where output cannot be counted.
Of the eight non-financial methods, delegation, consultation, empowerment and enrichment reach Herzberg's second scale. Rotation and enlargement do not.

takeaway: Piecework and commission replace the $360 basic and equal it; the other three add to it.
Delegation passes the AUTHORITY. Without it, nothing has been delegated.
Enrichment raises difficulty; rotation and enlargement do not.

notes.title: Leadership
notes.keyIdea: Management against leadership, the four styles, and why the move from entrepreneur to leader is hard.

items.text: Management — concerned with the work getting done. Authority comes from the post.
Leadership — concerned with where the firm is going. Authority comes from the person.
Autocratic — the leader, alone: the leader decides and tells.
Paternalistic — the leader, having explained: the leader decides, explains, and takes the staff interest into account.
Democratic — the leader with the staff: the leader decides with the staff, or lets them decide.
Laissez-faire — the staff, within a goal: the leader sets the goal and leaves the staff to it.
The four styles differ in ONE thing — who takes the decision — and run in that order from the leader alone to the staff alone.
Paternalistic still decides: the reasons are given and the staff's interests are weighed. Explaining a decision is not sharing it.
Laissez-faire sets the GOAL and leaves the method. A leader who sets no goal is absent, and the two look the same until something goes wrong.
From entrepreneur to leader: at 31 people staff must be recruited rather than known ($10,800 a post), decisions must be delegated, and authority starts coming from the post.
Which is the difficulty: the habits that built the firm — deciding fast, knowing everything personally — are the ones now in the way, and they have to go before anything has visibly failed.

takeaway: The four styles differ in who decides, and in nothing else.
Paternalistic explains and still decides. Explaining is not sharing.
The founder has to stop doing what made them successful.

quiz.question: A firm makes a machinist redundant rather than dismissing them. This means that:
options: the machinist failed to reach the required standard
the machinist is entitled to notice but not to redundancy pay
the firm will advertise the same post again within the month
the post itself is no longer needed
quiz.explanation: Redundancy is about the POST: the work has gone, so the job ceases to exist and statutory redundancy pay is due. Failing to reach a standard is a capability dismissal, which is about the person — and in that case the post remains and the firm does advertise it again.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a form of flexible workforce named in the specification?
options: Performance-related pay
Collective bargaining
Zero-hour contracts
A matrix structure
quiz.explanation: The five forms are multi-skilling, part-time and temporary, zero-hour contracts, flexible hours and home working, outsourcing. Performance-related pay is a financial method of improving performance, collective bargaining is a way of agreeing pay and conditions, and a matrix is a type of organisational structure.

quiz.question: A firm treats its staff as an asset rather than as a cost. The clearest sign of this is that it:
options: employs staff on contracts with no guaranteed hours
outsources work to whichever supplier quotes lowest
trains staff beyond what their current job requires
recruits externally so that it never pays for a promotion
quiz.explanation: Training beyond the immediate requirement is spending made in the expectation of a return — the defining move of the asset approach. Contracts with no guaranteed hours and outsourcing to the lowest quote are both ways of minimising the outlay, which is the cost approach.

quiz.question: A factory employs 25 machinists at $36,000 each and is considering outsourcing the work instead. The main effect on its costs is that:
options: the total cost of the work falls by $900,000 a year
a fixed cost of $900,000 a year becomes a cost that moves with output
the firm loses the ability to vary its output at all
training costs rise, because the supplier's staff have to be trained by the factory before they can start
quiz.explanation: Outsourcing replaces a wage bill the firm owes whether orders come or not with an invoice per garment, so the cost becomes variable. Nothing says the total falls: outsourcing is cheaper only when output is low or uneven, and dearer when it is high and steady.

quiz.question: Multi-skilling differs from job enlargement because multi-skilling:
options: gives one worker the capability to do several different jobs
adds more tasks of the same kind to a single job
pays a worker according to how many tasks they perform
guarantees a worker a minimum number of hours each week
quiz.explanation: Multi-skilling creates a capability the firm can draw on when it needs cover, so the worker can be moved between jobs. Adding more tasks of the same kind to one job is job enlargement, which changes the job rather than the range of jobs the person could do.

quiz.question: Which situation is best answered by temporary contracts rather than by multi-skilling?
options: Shirt orders fall by exactly as much as jacket orders rise
One machine is idle whenever its usual operator is absent
Skilled machinists are leaving for better-paid work elsewhere
Demand triples for three months each year and then returns to normal
quiz.explanation: A known, time-limited increase in the total work is exactly what a fixed-term contract matches. Demand moving between products and cover for absence are both about the same people doing a different task, which is what multi-skilling is for.

quiz.question: A firm negotiates one pay agreement with a union covering all its production staff. This is:
options: collective bargaining
the individual approach to employer relationships
a form of decentralisation
consultation as a non-financial method
quiz.explanation: One agreement negotiated by a union for all its members is collective bargaining. Consultation is asking staff before a decision the manager still takes, and decentralisation is about where in the hierarchy decisions are made, not about how pay is agreed.

quiz.question: Recruiting, selecting and training one supervisor on a $36,000 salary costs a firm $10,800. As a percentage of the salary, that is:
quiz.explanation: $10,800 ÷ $36,000 × 100 = 30%. 15% is the agency fee on its own, and 3% would be the advertising bill alone.

quiz.question: Which cost of replacing a worker usually appears on no invoice at all?
options: The fee charged by a recruitment agency
The output the new starter does not yet produce
The advertising placed in the trade press
The fee for an external training course
quiz.explanation: Lost output is a real cost that nobody bills the firm for, which is why turnover is routinely under-counted — here it is $1,800, the second largest item on the list. The agency fee, the advertising and the course fee all arrive as bills.

quiz.question: A firm fills a supervisor's post internally. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm has avoided recruiting altogether
A vacancy still has to be filled, one level further down
Induction training is no longer needed at all
The post can be filled without any cost to the firm
quiz.explanation: Internal appointment MOVES the vacancy rather than removing it: the promoted machinist has left a gap the firm must now fill. Some induction is still needed for the new role, and the promotion itself takes management time.

quiz.question: The main purpose of induction training is to:
options: teach a specialist technique that nobody in the firm currently uses
reward long service with a qualification the worker can take elsewhere
assess whether the new starter should have been appointed at all
reduce early mistakes and the time before a new starter is productive
quiz.explanation: Induction covers the job, the place, the people and the rules so that a new starter becomes safe and useful sooner and is less likely to leave in the first month. Teaching a technique nobody in the firm has is what off-the-job training is for.

quiz.question: Off-the-job training is more likely than on-the-job training to be chosen when:
options: the firm wants to avoid paying an external fee
output must not be interrupted for any reason
nobody already in the firm knows the technique being taught
the work can only be learned by standing next to somebody who is already doing it
quiz.explanation: Off-the-job training buys expertise the firm does not have, which is the one thing on-the-job training cannot supply. Avoiding a fee and keeping output going both point the other way, and work that can only be learned by doing it is the definition of on-the-job.

quiz.question: A firm has 5 levels in its hierarchy. Its chain of command is:
options: 5 links
4 links
6 links
2 links
quiz.explanation: The chain of command counts the LINKS between levels, which is one fewer than the number of levels: 5 levels give 4 links. Counting 5 counts the levels themselves, which is the commonest error in this sub-topic.

quiz.question: Each manager in a firm supervises 5 people, across 3 levels. How many staff does the firm have?
quiz.explanation: 1 + 5 + 25 = 31, which is (5^3 − 1) ÷ 4. 25 counts only the bottom level, and 6 is the same span over one level fewer.

quiz.question: A firm of 31 staff moves from a span of control of 2 to a span of 5, keeping every member of staff. The direct effect is that:
options: 9 staff are made redundant
the firm gains a level in its hierarchy
9 posts change from supervising to producing
every manager supervises fewer people than before
quiz.explanation: The headcount is unchanged in both structures — 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 and 1 + 5 + 25 both give 31 — so nobody leaves. What changes is that managers fall from 15 to 6, and a wider span means each remaining manager supervises MORE people, not fewer.

quiz.question: A firm is described as decentralised. This tells you that:
options: the firm has removed a level from its hierarchy
authority to take decisions has been passed down the hierarchy
each manager supervises a larger number of people
the firm operates from several different sites rather than from one head office
quiz.explanation: Decentralisation is about WHO DECIDES, and it is a separate choice from the shape of the chart: a flat firm can refer everything upward and a tall one can push authority down. Removing a level and widening spans are both facts about the hierarchy, not about the authority.

quiz.question: The defining feature of a matrix structure is that:
options: the firm has fewer levels than its competitors
every department decides its own budget
decisions are taken at the top and passed down
a member of a project team reports to two managers
quiz.explanation: A matrix lays a project across the existing functions, so somebody on it answers to the project manager for the project and to their function head for everything else. Fewer levels describes a flat structure, and where budgets are decided is a question about centralisation.

quiz.question: Flattening a hierarchy is most likely to REDUCE motivation for a worker who:
options: wants more say in how their own work is done
expects to be promoted within a few years
prefers decisions to be taken close to the problem
values being part of a team with a shared output
quiz.explanation: Removing levels removes promotions: a firm with 3 levels offers 2 steps up rather than 4. The other three are all things a flatter structure delivers more of, because 6 managers cannot take every decision for 31 people.

quiz.question: A firm cuts the number of workers it has to replace each year from 4 to 1, at $10,800 a replacement. Its annual saving is:
quiz.explanation: 4 − 1 = 3 replacements avoided, at $10,800 each, so $32,400. $43,200 is what the firm was spending in total rather than what it saves, and $10,800 is the cost of one replacement.

quiz.question: Taylor's scientific management rests on the claim that workers are motivated by:
options: pay
belonging to a group
recognition from their manager
the work itself being interesting
quiz.explanation: Taylor held that money is what motivates, which is why his method ends in a piece rate. Belonging is where Mayo and Maslow differ from him, and recognition and interesting work are Herzberg's motivators.

quiz.question: In Mayo's studies, output rose both when the working conditions were improved AND when the improvements were reversed. This suggests that what raised output was:
options: the level of lighting in the workshop
the length of the rest breaks
the attention the workers were given
the piece rate the workers were paid
quiz.explanation: Because output rose under both the change and its reversal, the conditions themselves cannot have been the cause — which left being noticed, consulted and treated as a group. This is why the claim that Mayo "proved money does not motivate" is wrong: he showed something else ALSO motivates.

quiz.question: According to Maslow, offering a worker the chance to redesign their own production line will motivate them only if:
options: they are paid more for doing it
the firm also offers them a promotion
their manager uses a democratic style
their lower-level needs are already met
quiz.explanation: The hierarchy is an order: a level only motivates once the one below it is met, so an opportunity aimed at the top level does nothing for somebody worried about pay or job security. Extra pay would address the bottom two levels and not this one.

quiz.question: Under Herzberg's two-factor theory, improving pay and working conditions will:
options: remove dissatisfaction without creating satisfaction
create satisfaction without removing dissatisfaction
create satisfaction and remove dissatisfaction together
have no effect on either satisfaction or dissatisfaction
quiz.explanation: Pay and working conditions are hygiene factors, and hygiene factors run from dissatisfied to NOT dissatisfied — satisfaction is on a separate scale reached only by motivators. Getting them wrong does real damage, which is why they have an effect at all.

quiz.question: A machinist is paid $1.50 for each garment completed. In a week of 280 garments the wage is:
quiz.explanation: 280 × $1.50 = $420. $360 is what 240 garments would pay, which is also the basic weekly wage — the two are set equal so that the comparison is about risk rather than about generosity.

quiz.question: A firm distributes 5% of its $111,600 profit equally among all 31 employees. Each receives:
quiz.explanation: 5% of $111,600 is $5,580, and $5,580 ÷ 31 = $180. $5,580 is the whole pool before it is divided.

quiz.question: Piecework and commission share which characteristic?
options: The payment is the same in every week
The payment depends on the whole firm's profit
The payment is decided by an annual appraisal
The worker carries the risk that demand is low
quiz.explanation: Both pay for output — units made or value sold — so in a bad week the worker's income falls with the work. A payment that depends on the firm's profit is a profit share, and one decided by an appraisal is performance-related pay.

quiz.question: A supervisor gives a machinist the week's orders and leaves them to decide the sequence. This is:
options: consultation, because the machinist was asked
empowerment, because the machinist has a standing authority
delegation, because the authority moved with the task
an instruction, because the supervisor set the orders
quiz.explanation: Delegation passes a task AND the authority to decide how it is done, which is exactly what choosing the sequence is. Consultation would leave the decision with the supervisor, and empowerment is a general standing arrangement rather than one task.

quiz.question: A packer who already packs boxes is also asked to label them. This is an example of:
options: job enlargement
job enrichment
job rotation
empowerment
quiz.explanation: Labelling is no harder than packing and carries no extra responsibility, so the job has become broader and not harder — which is enlargement. Enrichment would raise the difficulty and the responsibility, and rotation would move the packer to a different job.

quiz.question: Which non-financial method reaches a Herzberg motivator most directly?
options: Job enrichment, because it adds responsibility
Job rotation, because it relieves boredom
Job enlargement, because it adds tasks
Flexible hours, because they suit the worker better
quiz.explanation: Responsibility is one of Herzberg's five motivators, and enrichment adds it by changing what the job consists of. Rotation and enlargement both keep the difficulty and the responsibility the same, so neither reaches the second scale.

quiz.question: An appraisal raises a machinist's rate by 5% from $9 an hour. Over a 40-hour week the pay rises to:
quiz.explanation: $9 × 1.05 = $9.45 an hour, and $9.45 × 40 = $378. $9.45 is the new hourly rate rather than the week's pay, and $360 is the pay before the appraisal.

quiz.question: A manager announces a new shift pattern, explains in full why it is necessary, and adjusts it for the staff with the longest journeys. This leadership style is:
options: democratic
autocratic
paternalistic
laissez-faire
quiz.explanation: The decision never left the manager, so it is not democratic — but the reasons were given and the staff's position changed the outcome, which is not autocratic either. Explaining a decision and weighing its effect on staff while still taking it alone is the paternalistic style.

quiz.question: The four leadership styles in the specification differ from one another mainly in:
options: who takes the decision
how much the leader is paid
how many levels the hierarchy has
whether the firm is centralised
quiz.explanation: The four run in order from the leader deciding alone to the staff deciding within a goal, and that is the only dimension that separates them. Centralisation is about where in the hierarchy authority sits, which is a property of the firm rather than of the leader.

quiz.question: An autocratic style is MOST appropriate when:
options: the staff know the work better than the leader does
the firm wants to increase motivation without spending money
a decision must be taken immediately and staff are new to the work
the team is made up of experienced specialists
quiz.explanation: Speed and inexperience are the two conditions the style is for: asking people who do not yet know the work costs time and adds nothing. Where staff know the work better, or are experienced specialists, a democratic or laissez-faire style produces a better decision as well as a more popular one.

quiz.question: A leader tells a team the line must run 60 hours this week and leaves the pattern entirely to them. This is:
options: abdication, because the leader took no part in the decision
democratic, because the leader and the team decided together
laissez-faire, because a goal was set and the method left to the team
autocratic, because the leader set the hours
quiz.explanation: Setting the objective and leaving the method is the definition of laissez-faire; what separates it from absence is that a goal exists. The leader and the team did not decide together — the team decided alone, within a target it was given.

quiz.question: The move from entrepreneur to leader is difficult mainly because:
options: founders rarely understand the finances of a growing firm
a larger firm always needs a taller hierarchy than a smaller one
staff in a larger firm expect to be paid more than the founder
the habits that built the firm become obstacles once it is larger
quiz.explanation: Deciding everything personally and knowing every worker are advantages at four staff and bottlenecks at thirty, so the founder has to stop doing the things that worked — before anything has visibly gone wrong. Whether the hierarchy grows taller is a separate choice about span of control.

practice.question: Define the term 'redundancy'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate things to say, and the second is not a rewording of the first. Before writing, settle which half of the term does the work: plenty of people lose jobs, and only some of them are made redundant. An example will not substitute for either half.
Redundancy is the ending of a contract of employment because the POST is no longer needed (1 mark) — the work has gone, rather than the worker having failed — and it carries an entitlement to statutory redundancy pay (1 mark). An answer that says "when somebody loses their job" has neither half: it does not say what happened to the post, which is the whole distinction from dismissal.

practice.question: A firm recruits a supervisor on a salary of $36,000, working 200 days a year. It pays $1,200 to advertise the post, an agency fee of 15% of the salary, 20 hours of managers' time at $45 an hour, 5 days of induction, a $600 external course, and loses 10 days of the new supervisor's output. Calculate the total cost of recruiting, selecting and training this one supervisor, and express it as a percentage of the salary. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Seven figures, and only two of them are already in dollars — the rest have to be worked out before anything can be added, so do those first and set the sum out as a list. Appendix 6 advises showing workings for a Calculate, and here the workings are where the credit is: a wrong total with visible arithmetic is worth more than a right one with none. Work out the daily rate before you start, because two of the items depend on it.
The supervisor's day rate is $36,000 ÷ 200 = $180 (1 mark). The agency fee is 15% × $36,000 = $5,400; managers' time is 20 × $45 = $900; induction is 5 × $180 = $900; lost output is 10 × $180 = $1,800 (1 mark). Adding all six: $1,200 + $5,400 + $900 + $900 + $600 + $1,800 = $10,800 (1 mark). As a percentage of salary, $10,800 ÷ $36,000 × 100 = 30% (1 mark). A common slip is to use the manager's hourly rate for the induction days as well; the induction is the supervisor's time, not a manager's.

practice.question: A clothing manufacturer has 31 staff organised with a span of control of 5 across 3 levels. Construct an organisational chart for this firm, labelling the span of control and the chain of command. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Construct as requiring an accurately labelled diagram, so the labels are the command word rather than decoration on top of it. Work out the staff on each level before drawing anything, because a chart whose boxes do not add to the headcount is not the accurate diagram the command word asks for. Draw the levels first, then the joining lines, then the two labels.
One box at the top, 5 boxes on the second level and 25 on the third, joined by lines from each manager to the people reporting to them (1 mark). The boxes add to 1 + 5 + 25 = 31, which should be stated on the chart (1 mark). The span of control is labelled on a manager as 5 direct reports (1 mark). The chain of command is marked as a route from the top box to a bottom one and labelled 2 links — one fewer than the number of levels (1 mark). Labelling the chain as 3 is the commonest error here, and it is the one thing on the chart the arithmetic settles.

practice.question: A clothing manufacturer with 31 staff removes two levels from its hierarchy, keeping every member of staff. Explain one effect of this on the firm's wage bill. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Explain needs a cause and its effect, supported by knowledge, so decide which single effect you are following and take it all the way. The trap here is the word "keeping": nobody leaves, so any answer that saves money by reducing headcount has answered a different question. Work out what happens to the two KINDS of post instead.
Removing levels while keeping the staff means the remaining managers each supervise more people, so the span of control widens (1 mark). Managers fall from 15 to 6, so 9 posts change from a manager's to a machinist's (1 mark). At $72,000 against $36,000, each of those posts costs $36,000 less (1 mark), so the wage bill falls by 9 × $36,000 = $324,000, from $1,656,000 to $1,332,000 (1 mark). An answer that says the firm "saves on wages by employing fewer people" has missed that the headcount is unchanged.

practice.question: Analyse how Herzberg's two-factor theory explains why a pay rise may fail to improve a workforce's performance. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Analyse wants depth rather than breadth, so take one chain all the way instead of describing both theorists and both scales. The chain has to get from what pay IS in Herzberg's terms to a prediction about performance, and the step students miss is the one that says why a scale can run out. Appendix 6 says Analyse does not include evaluation, so a judgement about whether the firm should pay more is not being asked for.
Herzberg separates hygiene factors from motivators, and the two sit on separate scales rather than at the two ends of one (1 mark). Pay is a hygiene factor, so its scale runs from dissatisfied to NOT dissatisfied (1 mark). Once pay is adequate, the firm is already at the top of that scale, so a further rise has nowhere left to move the workforce (1 mark). Satisfaction is on the second scale, which only motivators reach — achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility and advancement (1 mark). None of those is affected by the size of the wage (1 mark), so effort and performance, which follow from the second scale, are unchanged (1 mark). A chain that stops at "pay does not motivate" has asserted the conclusion and skipped the two scales that produce it.

practice.question: A clothing manufacturer pays its machinists a basic wage of $360 a week and is considering moving them onto piecework at $1.50 a garment. Discuss the likely effects of this change. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 says a Discuss needs logical chains of reasoning IN CONTEXT showing causes and effects, with a brief conclusion — so the conclusion is required and should be one or two sentences rather than a full evaluation. Use the figures: they are what makes this a discussion of one firm rather than of piecework in general. Two chains taken properly will do more than four started.
At 240 garments the two systems pay the same $360, so this is a change in RISK rather than in average pay. A machinist producing 280 earns $420 and one producing 200 earns $300, so output and income now move together and the incentive to produce more is direct. The firm's wage bill also becomes variable, falling in a week when orders are low.
Against that: piecework pays for quantity and not quality, so rejects are likely to rise and the firm may need inspection it did not need before — a cost that offsets the gain. The risk transferred to the machinist is real, and in a slow week caused by the firm's own order book rather than by the machinist's effort, the pay cut is not an incentive but a grievance. On Herzberg's reading, pay is a hygiene factor, so a system that makes pay less certain can create dissatisfaction while adding nothing to satisfaction. The conclusion the figures support is that piecework suits this firm if its orders are steady and quality is checked; where orders are uneven, it moves a risk the firm is better placed to carry onto the people least able to.

practice.question: A founder whose clothing firm has grown from four staff to thirty-one still authorises every discount personally. Assess whether the firm should move to a democratic leadership style. (10 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a coherent chain of reasoning that considers the relative importance of factors and leads to a supported judgement — in Units 1 and 2 it carries 10 marks. The judgement is the part most answers leave out, and "it depends" is not one: say WHICH factor decides it and why. Plan two factors on each side and a decision before you write.
For the move: at thirty-one staff one person cannot take every decision without becoming a bottleneck, and discounts in particular are decided fastest by whoever is talking to the customer. A democratic style also delivers the non-financial motivators the firm currently has no access to — consultation, delegation and the responsibility that comes with them — at no cost in wages. And the founder's authority currently comes from being the founder, which is not transferable; a firm that has never taken a decision without them cannot function when they are away.
Against: a democratic style needs staff who know enough to decide, and staff who have never been allowed to authorise a discount have no practice at it. The first decisions will be worse than the founder's, and some will cost money. Speed also cuts both ways — consulting takes longer than deciding, and a customer waiting for an answer may not wait.
The factor that decides it is TRAINING rather than style. The firm needs the authority moved, because thirty-one people cannot be run from one desk, but moving it to people who have not been prepared produces the bad decisions that will be used as evidence the move was wrong. So the judgement is: yes, and in stages — delegate discounts within a stated limit first, train against the decisions that come back, and widen the limit as the judgement improves. A straight switch of style with no limits and no training is the version of this that fails.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that the most important factor in motivating a workforce is pay. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed, coherent and logical chains of reasoning showing a range of causes and effects, leading to a supported judgement. A 20-mark answer needs the theories used rather than described, the financial and non-financial methods weighed against each other, and a judgement that names the circumstances in which each side is right. Decide your line before you start and make every paragraph serve it.
The case FOR pay. Taylor's claim is that money is what motivates, and where output per person can be measured the evidence supports it: put a machinist on $1.50 a garment and output rises, because effort and income now move together. Maslow agrees about the bottom of the hierarchy — pay meets the physiological and safety levels, and nothing above them motivates until those are met, so a firm whose wages are inadequate cannot motivate anybody with responsibility or recognition. Pay is also the one method available to every job: a supervisor's output cannot be counted, but performance-related pay reaches them through an appraisal, adding $18 a week to a machinist's $360.
The case AGAINST. Herzberg puts pay among the hygiene factors, which run only as far as NOT dissatisfied: once pay is adequate, more of it acts on a scale that has already run out, and satisfaction is reached only by achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility and advancement. Mayo found output rising when the only thing that changed was the attention workers were given. And the non-financial methods that reach Herzberg's second scale — delegation, consultation, empowerment, job enrichment — cost nothing in wages, which means a firm choosing pay as its instrument is choosing the expensive option as well as the weaker one. Pay also has side effects that work against performance: piecework pays for quantity and not quality, and a profit share of $180 settled once a year rewards nothing anybody does this week.
The judgement. The question asks what is MOST important, and the honest answer is that pay is necessary and not sufficient, which is a different claim from either side of the view. Below adequacy pay dominates everything: a workforce worried about the rent is not motivated by responsibility, and no non-financial method will substitute. Above adequacy it is close to spent, and the methods that still have room to work are the ones that change the job. So the factor that decides which half of that answer applies is WHERE the workforce currently is — and a firm that has not asked that question will spend money on the wrong scale. The second thing the judgement has to name is the work itself: where output per person can be counted and is what the firm needs more of, pay-for-output is genuinely the strongest instrument available, and where it cannot be counted, pay reaches performance only through a judgement about the person, which is as good as the appraisal behind it and no better.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between treating staff as an asset and as a cost?
flashcards.back: Asset: spend on training, development and retention and expect the spending back as productivity and quality. Cost: minimise the outlay and replace people when they go. Which is right depends on how long the job takes to learn.

flashcards.front: Name the five forms of flexible workforce.
flashcards.back: Multi-skilling, Part-time and temporary, Zero-hour contracts, Flexible hours and home working, Outsourcing. Only multi-skilling keeps the same hours and the same people; outsourcing removes the employment relationship altogether.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between dismissal and redundancy?
flashcards.back: Dismissal is about the PERSON — conduct or capability — and the post remains, so it is advertised again. Redundancy is about the POST, which ceases to exist, and it carries statutory redundancy pay.

flashcards.front: What are the two approaches to employer/employee relationships?
flashcards.back: The individual approach: terms agreed with each worker separately, which suits rare or differing skills. Collective bargaining: a union negotiating one agreement for all its members, which suits many similar jobs.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between internal and external recruitment?
flashcards.back: Internal fills the post from inside — no agency fee, shorter induction, and a vacancy MOVED one level down rather than removed. External fills it from the labour market, here at a $5,400 agency fee plus $900 of induction.

flashcards.front: What does it cost to recruit, select and train one supervisor?
flashcards.back: $10,800 on a $36,000 salary — 30% of it. By stage: recruitment $6,600, selection $900, training $3,300. The $1,800 of lost output is the second largest item and appears on no invoice.

flashcards.front: Name the three types of training and what each is.
flashcards.back: Induction: given on arrival: the job, the place, the people and the rules. On-the-job: learning while doing the work, alongside somebody who already does it. Off-the-job: learning away from the work, on a course or at a provider

flashcards.front: What are the three purposes of induction training?
flashcards.back: Less time before the new starter is productive; fewer early mistakes, which in a factory means accidents and scrap; and fewer people leaving in the first month, each of whom would cost a full recruitment bill to replace.

flashcards.front: Define hierarchy, chain of command and span of control.
flashcards.back: Hierarchy: the levels of authority in a firm, from the top to the shop floor. Chain of command: the route an instruction travels down those levels, counted in links. Span of control: how many people report directly to one manager

flashcards.front: How many staff does a span of s over L levels reach?
flashcards.back: (s^L − 1) ÷ (s − 1). So (2^5 − 1) ÷ 1 = 31 and (5^3 − 1) ÷ 4 = 31 — the same firm, drawn two ways.

flashcards.front: How many links are there in the chain of command?
flashcards.back: One fewer than the number of levels. 5 levels give 4 links and 3 give 2. Counting the levels themselves is the commonest error in this sub-topic.

flashcards.front: What changes when a firm flattens its hierarchy but keeps every member of staff?
flashcards.back: Managers fall from 15 to 6, so 9 posts move from supervising to producing and the wage bill falls $324,000. Every remaining span WIDENS, and the promotions available fall from 4 to 2.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between centralised and decentralised?
flashcards.back: Centralised: decisions taken at the top and passed down as instructions. Decentralised: the authority to decide passed down the hierarchy. It is a SEPARATE choice from tall or flat — the chart shows the levels, not who decides.

flashcards.front: What defines a matrix structure?
flashcards.back: A project laid across the existing functions, so somebody on the project reports to two managers: the project manager for the project and their function head for everything else. Its one real cost is two managers claiming the same hours.

flashcards.front: By what four routes does motivation reach a firm's accounts?
flashcards.back: Productivity, retention, quality and absenteeism. Retention has the clearest figure: holding losses to 1 instead of 4 saves $32,400 a year.

flashcards.front: Name the four motivation theorists and their theories.
flashcards.back: Taylor — scientific management; Mayo — human relations theory; Maslow — hierarchy of needs; Herzberg — two-factor theory.

flashcards.front: What are the four steps of Taylor's scientific management?
flashcards.back: Study the job to find the quickest method; write that method down as the standard; train every worker to follow it; pay by the amount produced. The piece rate comes last because it is the incentive to follow a method that has to exist first.

flashcards.front: What did Mayo find, and what does he NOT show?
flashcards.back: Output rose when conditions were changed AND when the changes were reversed, so what mattered was the attention and the group. He does NOT show that money fails to motivate — he shows something else motivates as well.

flashcards.front: What are Maslow's five levels, bottom to top?
flashcards.back: Physiological → Safety → Social → Esteem → Self-actualisation. The ORDER is the claim: a level only motivates once the one below it is met.

flashcards.front: What is Herzberg's two-factor theory?
flashcards.back: TWO separate scales. Hygiene factors (pay, company policy, supervision, working conditions, job security) run from dissatisfied to NOT dissatisfied. Motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement) are the only things that reach satisfied.

flashcards.front: Name the five financial methods of improving performance.
flashcards.back: Piecework, Commission, Bonus, Profit share, Performance-related pay. Piecework and commission REPLACE the $360 basic week and are set to equal it, so the comparison between them is about risk; the bonus, the profit share and performance pay ADD to a basic wage.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between piecework and commission?
flashcards.back: Piecework pays per unit MADE — $1.50 a garment here. Commission pays a share of what is SOLD — 4% of sales. Both move the risk that demand is low onto the worker.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a bonus and a profit share?
flashcards.back: A bonus is an extra payment for hitting a TARGET the firm set: 10% of the quarter here, $468. A profit share is a fraction of the profit — 5% of $111,600, $180 each — so it is zero when the profit is, whatever anybody achieved.

flashcards.front: What is performance-related pay and where does it work?
flashcards.back: An appraisal raises the RATE itself: $9 to $9.45 an hour, $18 more a week, permanently. It is the only financial method available where output per person cannot be counted — a supervisor's, a designer's — and it is only as good as the appraisal.

flashcards.front: Name the eight non-financial methods of improving performance.
flashcards.back: Delegation, Consultation, Empowerment, Team working, Flexible working, Job enrichment, Job rotation, Job enlargement.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between delegation, consultation and empowerment?
flashcards.back: Delegation passes a task AND the authority to decide how it is done. Consultation asks before a decision the manager still takes. Empowerment is a standing authority over how the work is done, within limits — general where delegation is task by task.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between job enrichment, rotation and enlargement?
flashcards.back: Enrichment adds DIFFICULTY and responsibility, so it reaches a Herzberg motivator. Rotation moves the worker between jobs at the same difficulty. Enlargement adds tasks at the same difficulty. Only the first can motivate.

flashcards.front: Why does flexible working appear twice in this topic?
flashcards.back: Because the specification asks two different questions about it. Under approaches to staffing (1b) it is what flexible hours do for the FIRM: a wider recruitment pool and less premises. Under non-financial methods (4d) it is the CONTROL it gives the worker.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between management and leadership?
flashcards.back: Management is concerned with the work getting done and its authority comes from the POST. Leadership is concerned with where the firm is going and its authority comes from the PERSON. It is not a rank, and one person usually does both.

flashcards.front: Name the four leadership styles and who decides under each.
flashcards.back: Autocratic — the leader, alone; Paternalistic — the leader, having explained; Democratic — the leader with the staff; Laissez-faire — the staff, within a goal. They differ in that one thing and in nothing else.

flashcards.front: How is paternalistic leadership different from autocratic?
flashcards.back: The decision is still the leader's under both. Under a paternalistic style the reasons are GIVEN and the staff's interests are weighed in taking it. Explaining a decision is not sharing it, which is why it is not democratic either.

flashcards.front: What separates laissez-faire leadership from an absent leader?
flashcards.back: A goal. Laissez-faire sets the objective and leaves the method to the staff; an absent leader sets nothing. The two look identical from a distance until something goes wrong.

flashcards.front: Why is the move from entrepreneur to leader difficult?
flashcards.back: At four staff the founder is the structure: they decide everything and know everyone. At 31 staff must be recruited rather than known ($10,800 a post), decisions must be delegated, and authority has to start coming from the POST. The habits that built the firm are the ones now in the way.

mistakes.title: Using dismissal and redundancy as the same word
mistakes.looks_like: "The firm dismissed forty workers because demand had fallen."
mistakes.why: Demand falling removes the POST, not the person, so this is redundancy — and the difference is not a matter of wording. A redundancy carries statutory redundancy pay and a dismissal carries notice, so the two have different consequences for the firm as well as for the worker.
mistakes.instead: Ask what the firm does next week. If the post is being advertised again it was a dismissal; if it is not, the work has gone and it was a redundancy.

mistakes.title: Counting the chain of command in levels
mistakes.looks_like: "The firm has 5 levels, so its chain of command is 5."
mistakes.why: The chain counts the LINKS between the levels, and the number of steps between 5 points is 4. It is the commonest arithmetic slip in the sub-topic, and it shows up in a Construct as readily as in a Calculate.
mistakes.instead: Count the arrows, not the boxes: 5 levels give 4 links, and 3 give 2.

mistakes.title: Saying that delayering cuts staff
mistakes.looks_like: "Flattening the hierarchy let the firm reduce its workforce and save $324,000."
mistakes.why: The arithmetic says otherwise: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 and 1 + 5 + 25 both come to 31, so the same people are in both charts. What changes is that 9 of them stop supervising and start producing, and the saving is the difference in PAY between the two kinds of post.
mistakes.instead: Say what happened to the two kinds of post: managers fall from 15 to 6, so 9 × $36,000 = $324,000 comes off the wage bill at unchanged headcount.

mistakes.title: Treating a flat structure and a decentralised one as the same thing
mistakes.looks_like: "The firm flattened its hierarchy, so decisions are now taken lower down."
mistakes.why: They are independent choices. A flat firm can refer everything upward — 6 managers can still decide everything — and a tall one can push real authority down to the floor. The chart shows the levels and says nothing about who holds the authority.
mistakes.instead: Answer the two questions separately: how many levels are there, and who is allowed to decide? A question about one is not answered with the other.

mistakes.title: Writing that Mayo proved money does not motivate
mistakes.looks_like: "Mayo showed that pay is irrelevant and only social factors matter."
mistakes.why: His studies changed the conditions and then reversed them, and output rose both times — which shows that attention and the group ALSO raise output. It says nothing about pay having no effect, and Taylor's piece-rate results are not overturned by it.
mistakes.instead: Say what the studies showed: output rose under the change and under its reversal, so what mattered was being noticed and consulted. Herzberg is the theorist who separates pay from satisfaction, and his claim is narrower than "money does not motivate".

mistakes.title: Drawing Herzberg as one scale
mistakes.looks_like: "Pay runs from dissatisfied at one end to satisfied at the other."
mistakes.why: The two-factor theory is TWO scales, and collapsing them into one loses the whole prediction. Hygiene factors run from dissatisfied to NOT dissatisfied; motivators run from not satisfied to satisfied. Drawing one axis describes Maslow's fourth level instead.
mistakes.instead: Draw two lines. Hygiene: dissatisfied → not dissatisfied. Motivators: not satisfied → satisfied. Then say which scale the firm's proposal acts on — which is why $18 a week and job enrichment have different effects.

mistakes.title: Calling job enlargement job enrichment
mistakes.looks_like: "The packer was given labelling as well, which enriched the job."
mistakes.why: Labelling is no harder than packing and carries no extra responsibility, so the job is broader and not richer. Only enrichment raises the difficulty and the responsibility, which is what reaches a Herzberg motivator — and enlargement without either is often received as more work for the same pay.
mistakes.instead: Ask whether the DIFFICULTY rose. Harder and more responsible is enrichment; more tasks at the same difficulty is enlargement; different tasks at the same difficulty is rotation.

mistakes.title: Treating paternalistic leadership as democratic
mistakes.looks_like: "The manager explained the reasons to the staff, so the style was democratic."
mistakes.why: Explaining a decision is not sharing it. Under a paternalistic style the leader still decides — the reasons are given and the staff's interests are weighed in the deciding. A style is democratic only when the decision itself moves to the staff.
mistakes.instead: Ask one question: who decided? If the answer is the leader, it is autocratic or paternalistic, and what separates those two is whether the reasons were given and the staff weighed.

diagrams.description: IAL 1.3.4 · 4b names four theorists. Two of them have a canonical diagram: Maslow's five levels, which only motivate upwards from the bottom, and Herzberg's TWO scales, which is the whole of the two-factor theory.
checklist: Maslow: five tiers, physiological at the BASE and self-actualisation at the apex
Maslow: the order matters — a level motivates only once the one below it is met
Herzberg: TWO separate scales, not one axis with satisfied at each end
Herzberg: hygiene runs to NOT dissatisfied; only motivators reach satisfied
